source.filename: 2026-A coupled electromagnetic-mechanical model for high temperature.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Multilayer structure represented as multiple elastic thin shells satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis
Continuous displacement field constructed by extracting mid-plane displacements across turns based on deformation similarity
Neglect of induced electromotive force generated by current along the tape width (tape width inductance omitted)
Axial velocity assumed to be zero in time derivative of mutual inductance, retaining only radial velocity
Turn-to-turn mechanical separation neglected due to a 0.5 mm outer overband suppressing separation
Radial contact resistance varies solely due to deformation-induced changes in geometrical contact area, omitting contact pressure, preload, surface condition, and inter-turn friction
Normal layer treated with constant equivalent resistivity in parallel with the superconducting layer
Power-law E-J constitutive relation for superconducting resistive voltage
Linear elastic mechanical constitutive behavior with orthotropic/transversely isotropic equivalent elastic moduli and Poisson ratios
control_variables: Coil dimensions: 48 turns, inner diameter 25 mm, tape width 4 mm, tape thickness 0.1 mm, overband thickness 0.5 mm
Operating temperature: 4.2 K
Superconducting tape self-field critical current Ic0 at 4.2 K: 2120 A
Critical electric field Ec: 1 uV/cm
Normal layer resistivity: 0.552174 micro-ohm*cm
Equivalent radial contact resistivity rho_r: 1.6 micro-ohm*cm^2 for NI coil (1 ohm*m^2 for insulated comparison)
Base power-law index n: 31
Equivalent mechanical parameters: Er = 134 GPa, Ephi = 144 GPa, Ez = 144 GPa; Grphi = 48 GPa, Gphiz = 55 GPa, Grz = 48 GPa; Poisson ratios nurphi = 0.314, nuphiz = 0.3, nurz = 0.314
ODE solver tolerances: absolute and relative tolerances set to 1e-4
Split-field convergence tolerance: 1e-3 (max 10 iterations)
dependent_variables: Azimuthal current distribution and screening current density
Radial current and radial current density distribution
Coil voltage evolution
Inductance matrix coefficients and time derivative of mutual inductance
Displacement fields (radial ur and axial uz) and rotation angle alpha
Hoop strain distribution and maximum hoop strain
Critical current Ic distribution
Azimuthal magnetization loss power and power density
Radial Joule heating loss power and power density

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A multilayer structural continuum model based on elastic thin shells satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis was formulated to model coil deformation and interfacial slip under non-uniform electromagnetic forces.

The coupled electromagnetic-mechanical model predicts hoop strain difference with a 15.5% relative error against experimental measurements on a 3-turn REBCO coil under a 3.52 T field, compared to 70% error for an uncoupled model.
Deformation-induced rotation alters local perpendicular and parallel field components, mitigating critical current degradation and altering the mechanical strain evolution.
Electromechanical coupling suppresses maximum hoop strain from 0.457% to 0.35% during initial excitation, but amplifies maximum hoop strain from 0.456% to 0.481% after stabilization.
The study focuses strictly on high-temperature superconducting magnet coils and does not evaluate soft robotics, continuum robots, soft grippers, or variable stiffness mechanisms.

experimental_setup: Validation against experimental strain difference measurements from literature (Li et al., 2020) for a 3-turn REBCO insulated coil under axial magnetic fields up to 3.52 T
Numerical benchmark comparison with a 2D axisymmetric finite-element T-A formulation model under an external magnetic field ramp to 12 T and coil charging to 500 A
future_work: Incorporating a more detailed contact resistance description that accounts for local contact pressure, preload, surface condition, and inter-turn sliding
independent_variables: Time during external field magnetization ramp, stabilization hold, and coil charging
External magnetic field magnitude and ramp rate (up to 12 T)
Inserted coil operating current and charging rate (ramped to 500 A at 5 A/s)
Power-law index n-value (varied to test sensitivity)
Coupling mechanism modes (uncoupled, critical current effect only, inductance effect included, contact resistance effect included)
Radial and axial positions within the coil (turn number and height along tape width)
limitations_inferred: Thermal coupling is omitted; the coil is assumed isothermal at 4.2 K despite computed radial Joule heating and azimuthal magnetization losses, preventing thermal feedback into material properties.
The 2D axisymmetric formulation cannot model three-dimensional non-axisymmetric phenomena such as tape joints, localized defects, or non-uniform winding geometry.
The methodology was not applied to or evaluated on soft robots, continuum manipulators, soft grippers, or robotic variable-stiffness devices.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model adopts simplifications and does not capture practical details such as REBCO tape composite structure and inter-tape frictional behavior (Page 7).
Tape non-uniformities along length and width (such as local critical current variations) are not fully accounted for (Page 7).

Experimental validation was restricted to a 3-turn insulated coil without radial current paths, validating only steady-state strain without verifying transient radial current dynamics of NI coils (Pages 7-8).
The contact resistance model considers only geometric contact area variations from deformation, omitting local contact pressure, preload, surface conditions, and inter-turn sliding (Page 4).
Axial velocity is assumed to be zero in the mutual inductance time derivative to reduce computational complexity (Page 4).
Induced electromotive force generated by current along the tape width is neglected (Page 2).
main_results: The artificial neural network (ANN) calculates inductance coefficients with a maximum relative error of 0.01% and reduces computation time from 10,199 s to approximately 0.02 s per evaluation.
The coupled model achieves a relative error of 15.5% against experimental strain difference data under a 3.52 T field, outperforming the uncoupled model error of 70%.
Electromechanical coupling intensifies radial current bypass during coil charging and increases radial current density, especially in outermost turns.
Mechanical deflection modifies local field components, mitigating critical current degradation and causing shallower screening current penetration depth with higher peak azimuthal current density.
Coupling suppresses maximum hoop strain from 0.457% to 0.35% in early excitation stages but amplifies it from 0.456% to 0.481% after the system stabilizes.
The coupled model predicts higher local peak azimuthal magnetization loss power density and increased radial Joule heating loss compared to the uncoupled model.
Deformation-induced inductance variation is the dominant mechanism driving changes in radial current and shielding current distribution.
Higher power-law n-values increase the shielding current density concentration at coil ends, leading to increased local hoop strain.
modeling_methods: Axisymmetric partial element equivalent circuit (A-PEEC) model based on Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
Multilayer structural continuum mechanics model based on elastic thin shell theory satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis and incorporating interfacial slip
Artificial neural network (ANN) with dual hidden layers to compute quadruple integrals for mutual and self-inductance from the Neumann formula
Split-field iteration method coupling the circuit model in MATLAB (ode15s) with COMSOL finite-element magnetic and mechanical solvers
Power-law E-J relation for superconducting resistive voltage and magnetic vector potential (A-formulation) for magnetic field solution
Deformation-dependent critical current model incorporating magnetic field angle deflection and hoop strain degradation
performance_metrics: Inductance evaluation computation time: approximately 0.02 s (ANN) vs. 10,199 s (numerical integration)
Inductance coefficient relative error: maximum error <= 0.01%
Relative error in strain difference compared to experimental data: 15.5% (coupled) vs. 70% (uncoupled)
Maximum hoop strain suppression/amplification: 0.35% vs. 0.457% (early stage) and 0.481% vs. 0.456% (steady state)
Split-field convergence iterations per time step: typically 3 to 5 iterations
Loss power magnitudes: azimuthal magnetization loss power and radial Joule heating loss power
possible_gap_implications: The coupled continuum mechanics and electromagnetic circuit modeling approach could offer insights for modeling electromechanically active flexible structures, though adapting it to soft robotics would require large-strain kinematics and multi-material hyperelasticity.
Using neural networks to accelerate deformation-dependent electromagnetic integrals could be adapted to real-time control or simulation of magnetically actuated soft or continuum devices.
The omission of thermal feedback and contact friction indicates that comprehensive multiphysics modeling remains a challenge when simulating flexible electromagnetic mechanisms.
paper.research_objective: To develop an electromagnetic-mechanical bidirectional coupled numerical model for high-temperature superconducting no-insulation coils based on an ANN-accelerated circuit model and split-field iteration method, and to systematically analyze the multiphysics response (electromagnetic, mechanical, and loss behavior).
paper.research_problem: In high-temperature superconducting (HTS) no-insulation (NI) coils, shielding currents create non-uniform electromagnetic forces causing mechanical deformation, which in turn alters coil inductance and tape critical current; however, repeatedly recalculating the inductance matrix in coupled circuit models is computationally prohibitive using conventional numerical integration.
paper.title: A coupled electromagnetic-mechanical model for high temperature superconducting coils based on circuit model

source.filename: 2026-A global-local homogenization model for hierarchical chiral.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Small deformation assumption (axial strain eA <= 0.01, torsional strain tauA <= 0.01, bending curvature kappa <= 0.001)
Linear elastic constitutive relations for the helical constituent wires
Frictionless contact between helical wires under axial loading conditions
Uniform deformation along the wire arc length with negligible force and moment derivatives (dFn/ds = 0, dMn/ds = 0)
Circular wire cross-section simplification valid for large laying angles (beta in [79 deg, 89 deg])
Constant winding radius during deformation (R1 = R1_bar), ignoring Poisson effect and contact deformation on wire radius
Plane strain assumption for normal line contact deformation between adjacent wires
control_variables: Wire radius (Rw)
Young's modulus (E) and Poisson's ratio (nu)
Linear elastic strain boundaries (eA in [0, 0.01], tauA in [0, 0.01], kappa in [0, 0.001])
Finite element global mesh size of 0.07 with C3D8R solid elements
Laying angle operational range for circular section assumption (beta in [79 deg, 89 deg])
dependent_variables: Axial tensile stiffness (kee)
Torsional stiffness (ktt)
Bending stiffness (kbb)
Tension-torsion coupling stiffness (ket, kte)
Line contact stiffness per unit axial strain (kle) and unit torsional strain (klt)
Line contact force (Xn, P) and contact deformation (delta)
Coupling-decoupling coefficient (eta)
Axial resultant force (Fz) and twisting moment (Mz)
Elastic energy components (tensile, torsional, coupling, contact-induced elastic energy Wcon, and total strain energy W)
Contact pressure distribution and maximum Von Mises stress (sigma_Mises_max, sigma_Mises_el-max, sigma_Mises_con-max)
Variations in curvature (Delta kappa_b) and torsion (Delta tau)

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Hierarchical chiral helical structures possess tension-torsion coupling characteristics that serve as core foundations for programmable metamaterials, twisted soft actuators, and bio-inspired composites.

A global-local homogenization theoretical model based on Love's thin rod theory and strain linearization derives explicit closed-form stiffness components while accounting for interwire line contact forces.
Structural chirality dictates the sign of tension-torsion coupling stiffness and the direction of induced torque without altering axial tensile or bending stiffness.
A coupling-decoupling coefficient eta quantitatively defines the coupling state and identifies parametric boundaries where complete tension-torsion decoupling (eta = 0, ket = 0) occurs.
Line contact force per unit axial strain follows an inverse power-law scaling relationship with the number of helices (kle / (sin^2 beta_1 cos^2 beta_1) proportional to N1^(-1)).
Line contact induces localized stress concentrations, leading to higher maximum Von Mises stresses than predicted by classical homogenization models neglecting contact.
The proposed analytical homogenization model executes in seconds, compared to approximately 1 hour for a 3D finite element simulation of 1.46 x 10^5 elements on identical computing hardware.

Model stiffness predictions show agreement with prior experimental measurements for (1,3), (1,6+1), and (3,3) helical structures and match the Argatov model within 7% error across beta_1 in [60 deg, 89 deg].

Mechanically programmable series-parallel arrays combining opposite chiral units (RL and LR) achieve binary logic states (0/1), continuous 2D curve fitting, and complete isolation of axial load from torsional moment.
The analytical framework is bounded by small strain linearization, frictionless contact assumptions, and circular cross-section simplifications at high laying angles.

experimental_setup: Comparison and validation against previously published experimental stiffness data for first-order (1, 3) and (1, 6+1) strands and second-order (3, 3) cables from cited literature (Han et al., 2024; Han et al., 2025; Utting & Jones, 1987)
Three-dimensional finite element simulations using C3D8R solid elements with a refined global mesh size of 0.07 to simulate tension, torsion, and contact responses
Plane strain two-dimensional finite element contact model of two quarter-cylinders under compression to verify the normal contact force-displacement relationships
future_work: Incorporating tangential friction behavior into the homogenization framework to examine frictional dissipation under cyclic loading
Extending the theoretical formulation to hyperelastic constitutive laws suitable for soft fibrous hierarchical structures
Developing multi-level chiral array assemblies for complex mechanical signal encoding, high-precision curve reconstruction, and multifunctional mechanical logic operations
independent_variables: Laying angles of first-order and second-order helices (beta_1, beta_2)
Chiral winding configuration / laying direction (xi_1, xi_2: R, L, RR, RL, LR, LL)
Number of helical wires at structural levels (N_1, N_2)
Structural parameter / ratio of winding angles of adjacent helices (m = R_2 / (R_1 tan beta_1 cos beta_2))
Pitches of the helical structures (P_1, P_2)
Applied external loadings: axial tensile strain (eA), axial torsional strain (tauA), and bending curvature (kappa)
limitations_inferred: Physical prototypes of the proposed programmable metamaterial series-parallel arrays were not fabricated or experimentally evaluated in this paper; validation of decoupling logic is purely theoretical and numerical
The model does not incorporate dynamic effects, inertial forces, material viscoelasticity, structural damping, or fatigue wear
Geometric uniformity and perfect pitch along the length are assumed, without considering manufacturing tolerances, local strand clearances, or geometric imperfections
limitations_stated_by_authors: The theoretical framework is restricted to small deformations and strain linearization (eA <= 0.01, tauA <= 0.01, kappa <= 0.001) and cannot capture nonlinear responses arising from material plasticity or boundary nonlinearities
Large torsional strains may break the reciprocal symmetry of tension-torsion coupling stiffness (ket != kte) due to geometric nonlinearity
Large axial tensile strains induce plastic yielding and invalidate linear elastic constitutive laws
The frictionless contact assumption fails under combined tension-bending loadings or cyclic conditions where interwire stick-slip friction occurs
Circular wire cross-section simplification introduces error at smaller laying angles where sections deform into non-circular shapes
The framework does not account for hyperelastic material behavior necessary for soft fibrous hierarchical architectures
Poisson effect and contact deformation on the winding radius (R1 = R1_bar) are ignored
main_results: Derived closed-form analytical formulas for tensile, torsional, bending, coupling, and line-contact stiffness parameters of first-order and second-order chiral helical structures
Demonstrated that structural chirality determines the sign and direction of tension-torsion coupling and resultant torque while leaving axial tensile and bending stiffness unaffected

Established a coupling-decoupling coefficient eta to predict parameter combinations (such as large beta_2 and structural parameter m in RL cables) where complete tension-torsion decoupling (eta = 0) occurs

Identified a -1 power-law scaling relationship between line contact force per unit axial strain and helix number (kle / (sin^2 beta_1 cos^2 beta_1) proportional to N1^(-1)), enabling contact force tuning without altering wire radius or pitch
Revealed that contact-induced elastic energy and coupling energy proportions increase significantly as laying angles decrease
Showed that ignoring contact effects significantly underestimates peak Von Mises stresses on wire cross-sections, particularly at small laying angles and high external loads

Designed and demonstrated programmable series-parallel chiral helical metamaterial modules capable of binary mechanical logic (0/1), continuous function/curve fitting, and complete isolation/separation of axial force and torque

Demonstrated that the proposed analytical model reduces computational time to seconds compared to 1 hour for high-density 3D finite element models, maintaining consistency with FE and literature experimental data
modeling_methods: Global-local homogenization model based on strain linearization
Love's thin rod theory for curved rods in local Frenet coordinate systems
Johnson's Hertzian contact theory and plane strain elastic cylinder contact formulation
Kinematic analogy method for comparison of second-order helical kinematics
Three-dimensional finite element modeling (FEM) with C3D8R elements
performance_metrics: Stiffness prediction relative error compared to the Argatov analytical model (<7% error across beta_1 in [60 deg, 89 deg])
Discrepancy with the kinematic analogy method (~6% difference at m = 3, beta_2 = 79 deg)
Computational speedup (seconds for analytical homogenization model vs. ~1 hour for 3D FEM with 1.46 x 10^5 elements on an Intel Core i9-14900KF CPU)
Elastic strain energy partition ratios (tensile, torsional, coupling, contact)
Peak Von Mises stress and contact stress concentration magnitude
Target curve fitting error / decoupling load separation capability
possible_gap_implications: Although the homogenization model provides closed-form predictive rules for tension-torsion decoupling and contact stress in hierarchical chiral helices, applying these concepts to soft continuum robots or variable-stiffness twisted soft actuators requires extending the formulation to finite hyperelastic deformations, material viscoelasticity, and frictional contact, accompanied by physical robotic experimental validation.
paper.research_objective: To develop a linearization-based global-local homogenization model for hierarchical chiral helical structures that derives explicit closed-form stiffness expressions, elucidates the governing laws of chirality and geometry on tension-torsion coupling/decoupling, contact stresses, and strain energy partitioning, and enables programmable metamaterial architectures for curve fitting and load separation.
paper.research_problem: Existing analytical and numerical homogenization methods fail to simultaneously capture global tension-torsion coupling behaviors and local interwire contact stress/energy evolution across hierarchical chiral configurations, and lack parametric criteria for achieving continuous programmable regulation via precise tension-torsion coupling and decoupling.
paper.title: A global-local homogenization model for hierarchical chiral helical structures: Tension-torsion coupling and decoupling analysis

source.filename: 2026-Critical state model for superconductivity features and.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Current density magnitude must not exceed the critical threshold: |J| <= Jc(B), represented as a yield function fs(J) = |J| - Jc(B) <= 0
Electric field remains zero below the critical current density threshold (|J| < Jc implies E = 0)
The principle of maximum dissipation holds, stating that dissipation in the superconductor reaches a maximum among all permissible current states (E · (J - J*) >= 0)
Flow rule assumes isotropic collinearity between current density and electric field (E = \dot{\gamma} J / |J|)
Thermally induced flux creep is neglected in the critical state model (approximating the power law relationship as exponent n approaches infinity)
Constitutive relationship is smoothed via a trial current density J_trial = \sigma_s E regularized by a conductivity parameter and cutoff J = min(Jc(B)/(|J_trial| + \eta), 1) J_trial
Critical current density exhibits magnetic field dependence Jc(B) = Jc0 / [1 + (k^2 B_parallel^2 + B_perp^2)^(1/2) / Bc]^b
control_variables: Critical current density parameters (Jc0 = 2.8e10 A/m^2 or 1e10 A/m^2 or 3e8 A/m^2, k = 0.29515, Bc = 0.04265 T, b = 0.7)
Characteristic critical electric field threshold Ec = 1e-4 V/m
Numerical division-by-zero prevention parameter \eta = 1e-15 A/m^2
Discretization orders (second-order Lagrangian shape functions for magnetic vector potential A, constant/discontinuous order for current density J)
Penalty factor \rho_n for applying transport current constraints via an auxiliary ordinary differential equation
dependent_variables: Current density distribution J (or Jz)
Induced electric field distribution E
Magnetic field and magnetic flux density distribution B
Magnetization m and magnetic hysteresis curves
Electromagnetic energy losses
Global critical current of superconducting cables
Computational time and numerical convergence rate
Coefficient of determination (R^2) measuring fit against analytical solutions

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: The critical state model for type-II superconductors can be formulated within the framework of continuum mechanics and plasticity by casting the critical current threshold as a yield function and employing the principle of maximum dissipation to deduce flow rules and Kuhn-Tucker conditions.

Macroscopic vortex pinning in superconductors exhibits physical and mathematical equivalence to Coulomb friction stick-slip behavior, enabling classical contact mechanics regularization algorithms to resolve non-differentiable constitutive relations.

Spurious numerical oscillations in continuum field calculations across sharp gradient interfaces separating flux-flow and flux-pinning regions are eliminated by employing mixed-order finite element discretizations (second-order for magnetic vector potential and piecewise constant for current density).
The paper contains no experimental or theoretical investigation of soft robotics, continuum robots, soft grippers, or variable-stiffness actuation mechanisms.

future_work: Further development and improvement of the numerical implementation for transport current constraint conditions in the critical state model to mitigate stiffness matrix complications and improve efficiency.
independent_variables: Applied external magnetic field (Hext or Bext)
Applied transport current (Iext(t)) and charging rate (dI/dt)
Geometric dimensions of superconducting structures (film thickness d, width w, coil turns, cable layer counts, bulk dimensions)
limitations_inferred: The study is entirely theoretical and numerical; no physical experimental setup, fabrication, or experimental testing was performed.

The mechanical analysis is limited to analogies with continuum plasticity and friction; no coupled mechanical deformation, structural stress-strain states, thermal effects, or structural dynamics are modeled.
The study does not examine or address soft robotics, continuum manipulators, robotic grippers, or variable-stiffness mechanisms.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model still has certain convergence issues in loading and unloading calculations for complex structures, partly due to the effect of large penalty factors.
Transport current constraint conditions complicate the stiffness matrix structure, causing a decrease in computational efficiency compared to purely magnetized cases.
Thermally induced flux creep is neglected in the critical state model, which may deviate from realistic physical behavior when creep effects are significant.
The flow rule assumes an isotropic relationship where current density and electric field are parallel, which does not capture anisotropic double-critical-state behavior where they are non-parallel.
main_results: The proposed FEM A-formulation combined with Coulomb-friction-inspired regularization accurately reproduces Brandt's analytical solutions for superconducting thin films under magnetic fields and transport currents.

Using second-order Lagrangian elements for magnetic vector potential A and element-constant discretization for current density J successfully suppresses spurious numerical oscillations at steep gradient interfaces.

For superconducting coils, the critical state model yields current distributions, losses, and magnetization hysteresis loops matching the power-law model at high exponents (n=200) while approximating moderate exponents (n=38).
Computation time in coil magnetization simulations is reduced by nearly an order of magnitude relative to the T-A formulation, and is approximately halved in transport current simulations.

The model is successfully demonstrated on complex 3D/multiturn structures including CORC cables (24 tapes), quasi-isotropic cables (80 turns), twisted stacked-tape conductor cables, and bulk superconductors.
For bulk superconductors (benchmark 4 with n=201), the proposed formulation solves in 45 seconds compared to 1486 seconds for the H-formulation.
modeling_methods: Finite element A-formulation (magnetic vector potential) for Maxwell's equations
Continuum mechanics plasticity analogy using yield functions and the principle of maximum dissipation
Flow rule and Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) complementary conditions formulation
Coulomb-friction-inspired numerical regularization algorithm for non-smooth constitutive relations
Penalty function method converted to an ordinary differential equation with an auxiliary variable for transport current constraints
Mixed-order spatial discretization (second-order Lagrangian elements for A, constant discontinuous elements for J)
performance_metrics: Coefficient of determination (R^2) comparing numerical results against analytical solutions
Computation time (runtime in seconds) compared to T-A and H formulations
Model convergence and absence of spurious numerical oscillations in large gradient zones
Agreement of current density distributions, magnetic field profiles, losses, and magnetization loops against benchmark and power-law solutions
possible_gap_implications: Although this paper focuses strictly on superconductivity electrodynamics, the continuum mechanics formulation and friction-regularization methods developed for threshold-governed dissipation could potentially inform numerical modeling of dry friction, stick-slip, or non-smooth contact mechanics in mechanical systems, though their relevance to soft robotics remains completely unproven.
There is currently no demonstrated link between the critical state electromagnetic model presented in this paper and variable-stiffness mechanisms or soft continuum robotic devices.
paper.research_objective: To characterize the critical state model of type-II superconductivity from the perspective of continuum mechanics constitutive laws (using the principle of maximum dissipation, flow rules, and Kuhn-Tucker conditions), implement it numerically via a finite element A-formulation using a Coulomb-friction-inspired regularization scheme, and eliminate spurious numerical oscillations near large gradient regions using mixed-order discretization.
paper.research_problem: The critical state model for type-II superconductors is non-smooth, non-differentiable, and multivalued at zero electric field, making finite element modeling challenging; existing non-local integral formulations lead to dense matrices with poor computational efficiency (O(n_e^3.6)), and large current density gradients at flux flow/pinning boundaries cause spurious numerical oscillations and convergence failures.
paper.title: Critical state model for superconductivity: features and numerical implementation
